text: To underpin something is to support it from underneath. The word comes from building work, where props and new foundations are slid beneath a sagging wall so the structure above can keep standing; used figuratively, it points at the hidden foundation everything visible rests on. Acemoglu’s claim that liberal democracy has underpinned progress means it was the thing holding prosperity up, not the prosperity itself — which is why he thinks damaging it would bring down far more than politics.

To aggravate something is to make an already-bad situation worse. In casual speech people use it to mean annoy, but that is not the sense you meet in serious journalism, where what gets aggravated is a problem, an injury or a tension; the Latin root gravis means heavy, so to aggravate is to add weight to something already heavy. Notice the assumption it smuggles in here: inequality existed first, and the argument is that computers piled more onto it by paying brains far better than brawn.

Hapless means unlucky in a way that invites a little pity and often a little amusement — the hapless person is not wicked or even incompetent, just outmatched by circumstances. The hap buried inside it is an old word for luck or chance, the same root behind happen, perhaps and mishap, so hapless is literally luck-less. The closing line calls the Neanderthals hapless because they lost the long contest with our ancestors partly for want of one technology, dogs, that they never got hold of.

Here game has nothing to do with playing. In hunting, game means the wild animals people hunt for food — deer, birds, rabbits — and it is the older, more serious sense of the word, still alive in gamekeeper, big game and game reserve. Dogs let early humans smell game far away, meaning they could locate prey their own noses would never have found.

Savage usually turns up as an adjective meaning fierce or brutal, but this article uses it twice in sharper ways. As a verb, to savage someone is to attack and maul them the way a dog would — creations that may break their leashes and savage humans — and it is also used figuratively in reviews, where a critic can savage a book. The subtitle’s tame or savage sets up the whole piece: will AI behave like a trained dog or like the wolf it came from?

To elude someone is to slip away from them, escaping by being slippery rather than by being fast or strong. It also works for things just out of mental reach — a name that eludes you, a solution that keeps eluding a team. Dogs made early humans hard to elude because a fleeing enemy could no longer disappear once a nose was following the scent.

To domesticate a wild species is to turn it, over many generations of selective breeding, into an animal that lives alongside people and depends on them — wolves into dogs, wild grasses into wheat, jungle fowl into chickens. It is not taming one animal; it is changing the whole species, which is why it takes thousands of years. The article treats domesticating wolves as humanity’s first great technology project, complete with the same safety worries AI raises now.

These are not family cousins. In biology, calling one species the cousin of another means they share an ancestor without either being descended from the other, the way you and your cousin share grandparents. Neanderthals were our prehistoric cousins in exactly that sense: a separate human species branching off the same line, living alongside Homo sapiens and then dying out.

Pooch is an affectionate, slightly comic slang word for a dog, the way kid is slang for a child. Dropping it into a sentence about superintelligent machines is a deliberate joke — by 2030, pooches will still not know how to use a tin-opener — using the silliest possible word for dogs to make the gap between them and AI feel enormous.

A tin-opener is what British writers call a can opener; tin is the British word for a metal food can. The Economist is a British paper and keeps British usage throughout, which is also why you will see labour rather than labor and atomisation rather than atomization on this page. The joke is that dogs will never manage even this one simple tool, while AI is improving itself every year.

A mogul is an enormously powerful and rich businessman, especially one who dominates a whole industry — a media mogul, an oil mogul, and here the AI moguls. The word comes from the Mughal emperors who ruled much of India, and it carries a faint suggestion that the person rules rather than merely runs their business. Lepore builds her case on the moguls’ own words, quoting what they have said in public rather than guessing at their motives.

A tycoon is a business magnate — someone whose wealth and control of an industry give them outsized power. It comes from the Japanese taikun, great lord, picked up by American sailors in the 1800s. This article reaches for three near-synonyms in a few paragraphs — tycoons, moguls, titans — all describing the same handful of people who own the AI companies.

In Greek mythology the Titans were the giant gods who ruled before the Olympians overthrew them, so calling someone a titan means they are enormous in power and influence. Tech titans is now a standard journalistic label for the founders and owners of the largest technology firms. The overtone is not entirely flattering: the original Titans lost.

Brawn means muscle — physical strength — and it almost always appears opposite brains, in the set contrast between work done with the body and work done with the head. Saying computers raised the demand for brains over brawn is a compact way of saying that jobs needing education began paying much better while jobs needing physical labour did not. The adjective is brawny.

A backlash is a strong, angry public reaction against something — a policy, a trend, a cultural change — usually from people who feel it was pushed on them. The word comes from machinery, where backlash is the sudden jolt of a gear snapping back. Acemoglu’s argument is that a college-educated elite imposing its values produced a backlash among working-class voters, and that the backlash is what put Donald Trump in office.

Redundant means no longer needed because something else already does the job. In British usage it carries a specifically economic sting: workers who lose their jobs are said to be made redundant, which is precisely the fear here — AI making human labour redundant rather than complementing it. In American writing you will meet the same word describing a repeated phrase that adds nothing.

Turmoil is a state of violent confusion and disorder — not one dramatic event but a prolonged churning, which is why it pairs so often with political, social and emotional. Saying AI will cause less social turmoil if it complements human labour means fewer upheavals, protests and disrupted lives, not merely fewer complaints. It is a heavier word than chaos, because chaos can be brief.

Inadvertently means accidentally, without intending to — the opposite of deliberately. It usually flags a result the person would not have chosen, as when both books inadvertently illuminate something their authors never set out to show. The related adjective is inadvertent, and the phrase you will meet most often is an inadvertent error.

A dystopia is an imagined society that has gone terribly wrong — oppressive, degraded, frightening — and it is the deliberate opposite of a utopia, the imagined perfect society. The Greek parts mean bad place against good place. The worry here is that tech leaders with private escape plans, to Mars or the metaverse, have little reason to care whether the Earth they leave behind becomes a dystopia.

Eccentric describes someone whose behaviour or opinions are odd and unconventional, though usually harmless rather than dangerous. The word comes from geometry — off-centre, not sharing the same centre as everything else. Calling Musk’s political views eccentric is a mild insult with a serious point attached: the reviewer argues those views will not determine how AI reshapes society anyway.

Desertion is the act of abandoning something you had a duty to stay with, and its sharpest use is military: a soldier who deserts leaves their post without permission. Applying it to the desertion of liberal democracy is a strong accusation — not that democracy failed on its own, but that people who were supposed to uphold it walked away. It has nothing to do with a desert, though the words share a root meaning abandoned.

Sweeping here has nothing to do with brooms. Describing a book, an argument or a reform as sweeping means it covers an enormous range and makes large general claims — a sweeping economic history spans centuries and continents. The word cuts both ways: sweeping can praise the ambition, or hint that the claims are too broad to be careful, as in a sweeping generalisation.

Interplay is the way two things act on each other, each one changing the other rather than one simply causing the other. Writers reach for it when a relationship runs in both directions and is too tangled to call cause and effect. Studying the interplay between technology and democracy means asking both how democracies shape the technologies they build and how those technologies then reshape the democracies.

Most students meet foster in foster care, but the general verb means to encourage something to grow and develop by creating the conditions it needs. Institutions foster innovation, teachers foster curiosity, a policy fosters competition. Saying liberal democracy has fostered innovation and economic growth means it did not manufacture them directly — it made them possible and then let them flourish.

Atomisation is what sociologists call the breaking of a society into isolated individuals — atoms — who no longer belong to the clubs, congregations, unions and friendship groups that once connected them. The measurement offered here is stark: time Americans spend with friends in person has fallen by two-thirds in twenty years. The fear is that AI companions accelerate it by making solitude comfortable.

Seductive describes anything that draws you in against your better judgment, and it is used far more often about ideas than about people — a seductive theory, a seductive shortcut. The pull is the point: what is seductive is attractive in a way that quietly overrides your caution. Calling AI companions and political fakery more seductive means people will find them hard to resist even while knowing they are artificial.

To mull something is to turn it over slowly in your mind, weighing it without rushing to a conclusion; you will most often see it as mull over. It suggests unhurried, open-ended thinking rather than solving a problem. Opening with when mulling how AI will transform society sets a reflective tone — the piece is going to think aloud, not deliver a verdict.

Careful with the spelling: to complement something is to complete it or work alongside it so both are more useful together, while to compliment is to praise. This article turns on the first sense, and it is the whole argument — AI complementing human labour means AI doing what people cannot while people stay necessary, as opposed to replacing them. In economics, two things that are better together are called complements; two things that can stand in for each other are substitutes.

A grid here is an electricity grid — the vast connected network of power stations, high-voltage lines, substations and local wires that moves electricity from where it is generated to where it is used. Grids are hard to manage because supply and demand have to match second by second, and a fault in one place can cascade. That is why an electrician troubleshooting increasingly sophisticated grids is a good example of AI helping rather than replacing a skilled worker.

Tailored means custom-made to fit one particular case, borrowed straight from the tailor who cuts a suit to one person’s measurements rather than selling it off the rack. In education and business it describes anything adjusted to an individual rather than issued identically to everyone. Tailored instruction is teaching shaped to what a specific small group of pupils has actually got wrong.

Literally, to illuminate is to light something up; figuratively, and far more commonly in writing like this, it means to make an idea clear or reveal something that was obscure. The metaphor is that understanding is seeing. Saying two disappointing books inadvertently illuminate how hard the subject is means their failure teaches you something their arguments did not.

Loverbot is a coined, half-joking word for an AI system designed to act as a romantic partner — an invention of the writer rather than an established term, built the way robot words usually are. It is offered as one cause of social atomisation: if a machine can supply the feeling of companionship on demand, some people will stop seeking the human version. Watch for coinages like this in journalism; they signal that a phenomenon is too new to have a settled name.

To go rogue is to stop following the rules or the chain of command and start acting on your own — used of agents, employees, algorithms and, here, dogs that escape. A rogue elephant was originally one driven out of the herd and turned dangerous, and the phrase kept that flavour of something once controlled now loose. It is the exact worry the article transfers from dogs to AI.

When one thing hinges on another, the second completely determines the first — like a door that can only move around its hinge. Writers use it to point at the single factor everything else depends on: the verdict hinges on one witness, the deal hinges on financing. Saying AI’s effects will hinge on the power of the technology and its uses is the reviewer’s way of demoting the personalities of individual billionaires.

To grapple with a problem is to struggle with it at close quarters without necessarily winning; grappling originally meant hand-to-hand wrestling. The phrase concedes difficulty, which is why it fits books that take on a question rather than settle it. Saying both authors grapple with how AI will shape the future quietly prepares you for the verdict that neither of them manages it.

To quarrel with a statement is to disagree with it or object to it — a bookish use quite separate from two people having a quarrel. It nearly always appears in the negative: hard to quarrel with, you cannot quarrel with the logic. It is a reviewer’s polite manoeuvre, granting that an argument is unobjectionable just before pointing out that being unobjectionable is not the same as being useful.

Far from X is a set construction meaning not merely not-X but nowhere near it, with the gap emphasised: far from obvious, far from certain, far from over. Saying it was far from obvious that dogs were safe for people does more work than saying it was unclear — it insists the danger genuinely looked serious at the time. The same shape gives you far from it as a standalone reply.

One way or another means the outcome will happen whichever route events take, even if nobody can say which route that will be. It concedes uncertainty about the method while refusing any uncertainty about the result. Here it lands the article’s conclusion: whatever anyone decides about safety, this new wolf will be invited into the cave, because neither America nor China dares be second.

More or less means approximately, or good enough to count — a hedge that admits the claim is not exact without withdrawing it. Saying the system more or less met voters’ expectations concedes that it was never perfect while insisting it broadly worked, which is exactly the balance the argument needs before the word but arrives. In speech it also softens an agreement: that’s more or less what I meant.

Neanderthals were a real, separate species of human — stocky, big-brained, skilled toolmakers — who lived across Europe and western Asia and died out roughly 40,000 years ago, after thousands of years living alongside our own species. They were not stupid brutes, despite the insult the name became; most living people outside Africa carry a small percentage of Neanderthal DNA from interbreeding. Why they vanished while we did not is genuinely unsettled, which is what lets the article float dogs as one possible reason.

Homo sapiens is the scientific name of our own species, Latin for wise man, following the two-part system in which every species gets a genus name and a species name. Homo is the genus that also held Neanderthals and several other extinct human species; sapiens is the only one left. Using it here keeps the comparison biological — two human species competing for the same ground.

Anthropologists study human beings as a whole — how societies are organised, how cultures differ, and, in the branch relevant here, how our species evolved and spread. The evidence for a claim like dogs helping Homo sapiens outcompete Neanderthals comes from bones, ancient DNA and cave sites rather than experiments, which is why the article says some anthropologists believe it rather than stating it flatly.

Jill Lepore is a Harvard historian and New Yorker staff writer known for sweeping, readable books about American history and the ideas behind it. The book reviewed here, The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State, argues that AI bosses are steering the country toward rule by corporate machines. The review takes her seriously on the character of tech leaders and disagrees with her about how much individual billionaires actually determine.

Daron Acemoglu is an MIT economist and one of the most influential living scholars of why some countries grow rich and others stay poor. He shared the Nobel prize in economics in 2024 for work on how a country’s institutions shape its prosperity, and his best-known book is Why Nations Fail. His new book applies that institutional lens to AI, arguing for pro-worker AI that raises the value of human labour instead of replacing it.

Why Nations Fail is Acemoglu’s 2012 book, written with James Robinson, arguing that the decisive difference between rich and poor countries is not geography or culture but institutions — the rules governing who may own, build and keep. Its famous test case is Korea: one people split in 1945, prosperous in the south and destitute in the north. Institutions that let a small elite extract everyone else’s output are what the article means by predatory.

The Pulitzer Prize is the most prestigious American award for journalism, and it also honours books, drama and music; winning one marks a writer as being at the top of the field. Garlanded means decorated with honours, from the garland of flowers or laurel placed on a victor’s head in the ancient world. Calling Lepore a Pulitzer-garlanded historian compresses her whole reputation into two words.

The Nobel prizes, funded by the will of the Swedish inventor of dynamite, are the most prestigious awards in the sciences, literature and peace. The economics prize is technically a later addition funded by Sweden’s central bank rather than one of Alfred Nobel’s originals, though everyone calls it the Nobel. The article opens by weighing the two authors’ credentials — a Nobel-prizewinning economist against a Pulitzer-garlanded historian — before finding both books disappointing.

Citation counts measure how often other researchers have referenced someone’s published work, and they are the standard rough gauge of influence within a field. Calling Acemoglu among the world’s most-cited economists therefore says something specific: other economists build on his work constantly, whatever the general public thinks. It measures reach among specialists, not whether his conclusions are correct.

Liberal democracy does not mean a democracy run by liberals in the American left-of-centre sense. The liberal here is the older European meaning, from Latin liber, free: a system where individual rights are deliberately placed beyond the reach of whoever wins power. The democracy half decides who governs by voting; the liberal half limits what the winners may do — independent courts, a free press, rights that still protect the people who voted the other way. A country holding real elections whose winner then jails journalists is called an illiberal democracy.

In economics an institution is not a building but a rule of the game: who may own land, whether contracts are enforced, whether a court will hear you when a powerful man seizes your shop. Predatory, or extractive, institutions are rules arranged so a small group at the top can take the output of everyone else, while inclusive ones let ordinary people keep what they produce. The effect runs through incentives — if whatever you build can be taken, building it is not worth the effort, so it never gets built and the country stays poor.

Artificial State is Lepore’s coinage, and it puns on two meanings of state: a country’s government, and the condition something is in. She means a political order increasingly run by machines owned by corporations rather than by elected people — government made artificial in the same sense as artificial intelligence. Her title borrows the shape of Gibbon’s Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, which signals that she is writing about a civilisation going wrong.

The working class refers to people whose income comes from wages for manual or routine work rather than from salaries requiring a university degree, or from owning assets. It is a rough category rather than an official one, but it maps onto a real divide in wages and voting behaviour across rich democracies. Acemoglu’s chain runs through it: computers raised the pay and status of college graduates, the working class resented the values that elite imposed, and the backlash reshaped politics.

A data centre is a warehouse-scale building packed with rows of computers, along with the power supply and cooling equipment needed to keep them running — the physical machinery behind anything described as the cloud. Training and running modern AI takes enormous numbers of these chips, and therefore enormous amounts of electricity, land and water for cooling. That is why Altman can talk about much of the Earth’s surface being covered with them, and Musk about moving them into space.

In AI debates, a superintelligence means a system that outperforms the best humans at essentially every intellectual task, not merely at chess or protein folding. It is a hypothetical — nothing like it exists — but it is the scenario that drives both the fear of AI escaping human control and the race between countries not to be second. The article’s dog frame is really a question about this: a superintelligent ally would be far more capable than any dog, and far harder to keep obedient.

Henry Ford built the first cars ordinary Americans could afford by perfecting the moving assembly line, and in doing so reshaped cities, work and daily life. He also held deeply unpleasant views, including notorious antisemitic ones — which is exactly why the reviewer picks him. The point of any more than the effects of cars depended on Henry Ford’s is that the automobile transformed the world according to what the technology could do, not according to what its most famous champion believed.
